title: MB9-08947
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, the appellant and a citizen of Chad, is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his refugee protection claim for lack of credibility. a.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, the appellant and a citizen of Chad, is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his refugee protection claim for lack of credibility. a. In his Basis of Claim Form1 (BOC Form), the appellant alleges that he is a member of the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (XXXX) [XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX] and that he participated in a demonstration for the release of the former leader, Médard Laoukein. During an XXXX meeting the day after the demonstration, the police and the Agence nationale de sécurité (ANS) [national security agency] raided the premises, arrested members, and seized documents, including the list of members. The appellant managed to flee and sought refuge with a cousin. There, he learned that the ANS was searching for all members who had not been arrested. He left Chad with an American visa and filed a refugee protection claim in Canada on August 21, 2017. If he were to return to Chad, he fears that the ANS will incarcerate, torture, and kill him. b. In its decision, the RPD found that the appellant's account was not credible due to the issues in the documents submitted into evidence that cast doubt on their authenticity, and because the appellant's behaviour was inconsistent with that of a person wanted by the ANS and fearing for his life. c. In his memorandum, the appellant argues that the RPD lacked flexibility in its assessment of the evidence and erred in its assessment of his credibility by concluding that his behaviour was inconsistent with that of a person who fears for his life. d. The determinative issue is the appellant's credibility.
Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD's determination.
The role of the RAD is to review RPD decisions while applying the correctness standard of review after conducting an independent analysis of the evidence on the record.2

After applying the standard of correctness, listening to the recording of the hearing held before the RPD, and reviewing the evidence, as well as the appellant's arguments, I am of the opinion that the RPD did not err in its assessment of the appellant's credibility. My reasons are as follows. Errors in the documentary evidence

In its decision, the RPD considered that the documents submitted into evidence by the appellant contain a sufficient number of errors to cast doubt on their truthfulness and authenticity. For example, the letter from the official spokesperson of XXXX3 stating that the appellant was a member of the association featured neither a letterhead nor the association's or author's contact information. This letter, dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019, and submitted by the appellant to support his refugee protection claim, did not include any information about the police raid on the premises, the arrests of members or that the ANS had a list of members.
The RPD also noted that the XXXX seal, which appears on two documents4 submitted by the appellant to establish his membership, contains several spelling errors.

In his memorandum, the appellant argues that he must benefit from the presumption of truthfulness.5 He claims that the RPD lacked flexibility with regard to the format of the documents and was hasty in its decision with respect to the truthfulness of the documents. He adds that since XXXX is an underground association, it was normal for the documents to contain shortcomings in terms of their formality and contact information.

I carefully listened to the recording of the hearing before the RPD. I was of the view that the appellant's testimony regarding the shortcomings in the documents was vague and confused. He was unable to provide explanations for the deficiencies that the RPD noted.

The errors noted by the RPD in the documents provide sufficient reasons to doubt the appellant's credibility. These errors are numerous and significant and the appellant's explanations are unsatisfactory. The lack of detail in the XXXX spokesperson's letter regarding the circumstances of the problems that the appellant was subjected to is particularly concerning, given that this document was submitted by the appellant to support his refugee protection claim. The RPD's finding that the errors in the documents undermine the appellant's credibility is correct and well supported by the evidence.

Where the claimant's personal testimony is not credible, it is reasonable for the RPD to have credibility concerns with the supporting documentary evidence and it may give it minimal weight.6 Contradictory testimony that is not credible with respect to the details

The appellant testified that he participated in a demonstration on XXXX XXXX for the release of the former leader, XXXX XXXX, who was arrested the XXXX XXXX, namely July 14. However, a newspaper article submitted by the appellant reports that Mr. XXXX was arrested on July 13. When the RPD asked the appellant about this inconsistency, he initially answered that he had another article which stated that it was the XXXX, but that he did not submit it into evidence.7 Once this article was exhibited by the appellant's counsel, the article in question was also dated XXXX XXXX. The appellant then adjusted his testimony and stated that it was not until XXXX XXXX that he learned of Mr. XXXX arrest.8 This confusion continues throughout his BOC Form, where he states that on [translation] "XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, we held a meeting," though it was clearly XXXX. Furthermore, in a letter written by his uncle, the latter writes that the demonstration took place on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017.9 When confronted with this, the appellant admitted to the letter's contents, but added that his uncle had meant that the events began on the XXXX.

In his memorandum, the appellant argues that the errors in the dates are minor and that he should have been given the benefit of the doubt. I respectfully disagree. The recording of the hearing establishes that the appellant contradicted his own documentary evidence and adjusted his confused testimony. This undermines his credibility.

The Federal Court recognized that, while the discrepancies and contradictions considered individually might have seemed insignificant, when taken together and considered in context, they may support a finding of lack of credibility.10

Another point of confusion concerns the appellant's testimony about XXXX itself. The appellant alleged that he had been a member for one year; but, according to his testimony, he did not know who the leaders were or the names of the ten or so other members of the association. Surprisingly, he also did not know who was in charge of the organization or who organized the activities. The appellant did not know the names of those arrested during the demonstration or following the police raid on the premises (two or three people). He testified in a very general manner that the organization's goal was to improve conditions for the Chadian population, without providing more detail. The appellant's inability to provide sufficient details about the association he claims to belong to suggests that the appellant was not an active participant and that he does not have much knowledge of the XXXX. The appellant's vague answers are not consistent with what is reasonably expected from an active member, which the appellant claims to be. Once again, this undermines his credibility. Inconsistent behaviour and subjective fear

The RPD found that the appellant's behaviour, following the police raid of the XXXX premises during a meeting of its members, was inconsistent with that of someone who fears for his life. At the time that the events took place, the appellant had a Schengen visa, specifically for France. However, rather than leaving as soon as possible, the appellant decided to stay in Chad to apply for a visa to the United States, which for the RPD showed a lack of subjective fear.

When the RPD asked the appellant about the potential risk that he faced by delaying his departure to potentially obtain an American visa, the appellant testified that France was too close to Chad, that he had heard about undercover ANS officers being in France and that, regardless, he wanted to come to Canada.

I am of the opinion that the appellant's behaviour and his answers are not at all acceptable in the circumstances. He alleges that the ANS is looking for him, yet he took risks by staying in Chad and by travelling to the United States Embassy at least twice to complete documents and have his fingerprints taken for his visa.11

A review of his passport12 shows that the appellant took a direct flight from N'Djamena to Paris and stayed there for two days before travelling to Casablanca and then the United States. This behaviour contradicts his explanation that he wanted to avoid France because of the presence of ANS undercover operatives and the risk of being caught there, details for which he provided no evidence other than hearsay.

Failure to apply for asylum at the first opportunity has consistently been considered as a sign of a lack of subjective fear, undermining the refugee protection claimant's credibility.13 In this case, the appellant took a flight to Paris and spent two days there before going to Morocco. He failed to satisfactorily explain why he did not apply for asylum in France despite having a visa and having travelled there voluntarily. The RPD's conclusion that his behaviour was inconsistent with that of someone who fears for his life is correct. I have no cause to intervene.

International protection under the Convention is a surrogate protection for those who face a persecution threat. Asylum shopping is incompatible with the surrogate dimension of international refugee protection. The Convention exists to help people who need protection, rather than to help people who simply prefer one country over another.14

During his submissions at the end of the hearing,15 the appellant referred to the National Documentation Package on Chad,16 specifically tabs 2.1 and 4.6, which report on arbitrary murders committed by the authorities, the torture and surveillance of people who participate in demonstrations, and how the government treats those who oppose the regime, in order to support his allegations of fear of persecution and threats to his life.

The documentary evidence regarding country conditions does not in itself establish the existence of a well-founded fear of persecution. The onus was on the appellant to establish a connection between the documentary evidence reporting on the problematic situations in his country and his personal situation, which he failed to do in this case.

After considering all the evidence and conducting my own independent assessment of the record, I am of the opinion that the RPD's decision is correct. The accumulation of inconsistencies and contradictions caused a fatal blow to the appellant's credibility.
For these reasons, I confirm the RPD's determination that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is not a Convention refugee pursuant to section 96 or a person in need of protection pursuant to section 97 of the IRPA.

The appeal is dismissed.
